extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, federal judges, litigators, and advanced law students interested in separation of powers and federal-court practice
extracted.subtask_description: An academic analysis and normative prescription about how federal courts — especially lower courts — review and check a category of executive action the author calls “enforcement lawmaking,” including the managerial, doctrinal, and remedial tools courts use. It documents practices (case management, discovery, appointment, remedies) and doctrinal developments (standing, ripeness, nationwide injunctions) and advises Supreme Court restraint to permit percolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement Lawmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The exercise of enforcement discretion in a manner that goes beyond simple policy and that shares attributes of law — executive actions that ‘look like lawmaking’ through systemic enforcement or nonenforcement decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition and scope: occurs when the President or executive branch tailors enforcement in ways that reform law or create policy effects (examples: DACA, transgender bathroom/military policies, southern border wall, sanctuary cities, census citizenship question). The Article argues this category merits distinct attention because it is responsive to congressional inaction and can be subject to judicial oversight across multiple doctrinal dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managerial Checks (ordinary case management as transparency and public accountability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary leverages ordinary case-management powers to force transparency on the Executive and hold it to account in suits challenging enforcement lawmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes routine orders and judicial tools that make executive decisionmaking visible: discovery orders, timing and scheduling, conferences, recordkeeping, and routine interlocutory orders. Managerial checks render the mere existence of judicial review powerful by creating public visibility into executive rationales and processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery as a Managerial Tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of discovery to obtain executive branch information and justification (e.g., ordering depositions of high-level officials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York v. U.S. Dep’t of Commerce — district court ordered the Secretary to sit for a deposition concerning the citizenship question on the census. Discovery orders can expose internal deliberations, constrain thin justifications, and shape later merits review; they are a key managerial mechanism to compel transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case Management and Routine Orders (timing; conferences; judicial notice; amicus participation; attorney withdrawals; post-trial management)
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine interlocutory and case-management practices that structure litigation against the Executive and affect the flow of information, public participation, and the durability of relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific managerial sub-practices discussed: timing of litigation and scheduling; holding conferences; judicial notice practices; facilitating amicus participation; rules and scrutiny on attorney withdrawals (e.g., requiring reasons); and post-trial management (enforcement and implementation of relief). These ordinary orders collectively function as tools of accountability and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of Defenders and Reliance on Non-Parties (intervention; appointment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts’ power to appoint amici, counsel, or special masters and to permit intervention shapes litigation and can act as a check on executive action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include appointment of amicus curiae to argue against government positions (United States v. Flynn), appointment to manage criminal contempt, and intervention rules allowing nonparties to participate. Guidance emphasizes courts’ ability to rely on non-party actors to preserve the integrity of the judicial forum and ensure adversarial testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-enforcement Challenges / Ripeness (timing shapes substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts increasingly entertain pre-enforcement (pre-enforcement posture) challenges to executive action, holding that litigation can be justiciable before formal enforcement steps occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: suits challenging transgender military/service bans brought pre-enforcement. The Article notes that redefining ripeness to permit earlier review changes when and how courts can scrutinize enforcement lawmaking and that timing can shape legal doctrines and remedies available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justiciability and Article III Standing (structuring suits challenging enforcement lawmaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing, ripeness, and other justiciability doctrines are being adapted to shape who can sue and when in suits addressing enforcement lawmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article treats standing as the ‘who’ of judicial review and documents doctrinal developments opening courts to multi-actor coalitions (states, private parties, associations, Congress). It stresses that changes in standing doctrine structure separation-of-powers litigation and expand the availability of federal litigation as a check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political Cases and the Tension from Caution to Politics
rubrics_metrics.description: The categorization of some suits as ‘political cases’ affects courts’ willingness to adjudicate enforcement lawmaking claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article observes that executive defendants have argued ripeness and political-question barriers to keep such matters out of court, while lower courts have sometimes been willing to reach separation-of-powers questions rather than avoid them. The doctrinal friction between caution (nonjusticiability) and political engagement is a recurring axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional Participation and Standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Houses of Congress or congressional actors can participate in litigation to assert institutional interests and influence separation-of-powers disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the House suing the Executive over ACA implementation. The Article discusses how courts have handled congressional participation and standing claims and how courts may augment Congress’s voice through procedural and remedial accommodations.

rubrics_metrics.name: States as Anchors for Suit (recognizing state standing)
rubrics_metrics.description: States often serve as plaintiffs to anchor suits against executive action; courts have developed state-focused standing theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two state standing routes are emphasized: (a) recognizing broad pecuniary injuries (economic/financial harms to states), and (b) recognizing new sovereign injuries (assertions of state sovereign interests). The Article documents lower-court developments that make state litigation a central mechanism for checking enforcement lawmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice Without Standing (parties without Article III standing; alternative participation vehicles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms by which actors influence litigation and separation-of-powers debates even if they lack Article III standing in the traditional sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described vehicles include amici, parties functioning like ‘parties without standing,’ and procedural avenues through which non-litigant actors (states, associations, or congressional entities) can augment the institutional voice in litigation and help structure remedies and factual records.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Remedial Authority: The Rise and Controversy of the Nationwide Injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts have increasingly used nationwide injunctions to enjoin executive action across the country; this remedy has provoked doctrinal and policy debates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government criticisms: nationwide injunctions limit percolation, create mootness and conflicting-obligation problems, and may exceed judicial power. Lower courts generally accept authority to issue such injunctions but recognize prudential limits. The Article frames the central question as what limits should apply rather than whether the remedy is ever permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percolation and the Value of Diffuse Decisionmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing multiple lower-court decisions to develop law (percolation) has institutional benefits — improved accuracy, legitimacy, and reduced groupthink — that counsel deferential treatment toward lower-court development of novel doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: diffusion across districts and circuits reduces capture and polarization, allows diverse decisionmakers to refine doctrine over time, and yields better-tested legal rules. The Article argues the Supreme Court should be cautious about early intervention so that percolation can occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shadow Docket and Extraordinary Relief: Effects on Legitimacy and Forum
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court’s frequent grant of emergency relief on the shadow docket in cases challenging executive action affects perceptions of lower-court legitimacy and creates expectations about extraordinary relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical observation: shadow-docket grants often favor the Solicitor General and halt discovery or enforcement pending appeal. The Article warns that special treatment on the shadow docket can undermine confidence in district courts and short-circuit percolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Subjugation of Judicial Power to Executive Power (Supreme Court supervisory role — A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court should avoid prematurely dictating boundaries of judicial power from above in ways that subordinate the judiciary to the Executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative prescription: allow lower courts freedom to fashion checking tools; avoid interventions that ‘subjugate’ judicial power by limiting district courts’ managerial and remedial experimentation early in doctrinal development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avail Itself of the Benefits of Diffuse Decisionmaking (Supreme Court supervisory role — B)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court should recognize the institutional benefits of diffuse decisionmaking and permit percolation before resolving contested questions about judicial power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: the Court should value percolation, avoid rushing to the merits on institutional questions, and consider the competence of district courts as case-management experts. Diffusion helps build legitimacy and reduces polarization from single-court resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit the Judicial Power to Evolve (Supreme Court supervisory role — C)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court should allow the judicial power to develop incrementally through lower-court practice rather than fix doctrinal boundaries too early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article argues that judicial power is dynamic; district courts, with expertise in case management and justiciability, are well positioned to refine doctrines (standing, ripeness, remedies). The Court should be solicitous of lower-court views on the core of judicial power and intervene selectively.
